newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia plans to limit election campaigning.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia plans to limit election campaigning.

text.p: The Indonesian body empowered by President Suharto to draw up guidelines for election campaigning has suggested limiting outdoor rallies for next year's parliamentary polls, the Jakarta Post reported on Tuesday.

Retired Lieutenant-General Soekarto, secretary-general of the National Council for Defence and Security, was quoted as saying outdoor campaigning should still be allowed but with strict limits aimed at preventing violence.

The council has said that convoys of political supporters on motorcycles or trucks should be banned and replaced by assemblies for speeches and discussions at sites decided by advisers and the General Elections Institute.

During the run-up to the last general elections in 1992, traffic in the capital Jakarta was often jammed for hours as tens of thousands of political supporters took to the streets in convoys every day during the campaign.
"Campaign sessions in the past general elections have often been marked by brutality...(and)...violations of electoral laws," Soekarto was quoted as saying.
"We need to minimise the possibilities of clashes among supporters of the political contestants," he said.

Soekarto was speaking after meeting leaders of the three official political parties, the ruling Golkar, Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) and the Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democractic Party (PDI).

The council, made up of retired military officers who advise the president on state matters, said convoys carrying party supporters should include not more than 10 cars and move at intervals of three minutes.
Suharto last month called for new regulations on election campaigning to prevent a repetition of past election chaos and violence.

Indonesia's tightly controlled election campaign is scheduled to begin on April 29 and end on May 23. There is usually a cooling-off period of seven days before election day, but no dates have yet been announced.
The council has suggested a five-day cooling off period.
